Yet, with a scholar's peculiar detachment, he found himself wishing the tedious preliminaries were concluded, his absurd sentence pronounced, and his fate, whatever monstrous form it might take, irrevocably sealed, since it was clear no less would satisfy the grim-faced assembly. For the swift conclusion of this charade, he had not long to wait; the interminable roll-call of the court's illustrious, if somewhat bewildered, members seemed to gallop to an end, and they had scarcely settled into their velvet cushions when a hush, like that preceding a thunderclap, fell over the hall. Everybody appeared to be in better humor, too, after the tedious procession, save for the Empress and the Master of Revels; the former, a vision of regal indifference, looked even more like a statue carved from moonstone than usual, her gaze fixed on some point beyond the furthest star; whilst the latter, a grotesque figure in motley, was performing a silent, anticipatory jig of delight, which was, as all in the court knew, the very worst possible harbinger of good fortune.

The Grand Vizier, a man whose voice was as voluminous as his robes, and whose self-importance swelled like an ill-made pastry, cleared his throat with a sound like a distant avalanche, and gestured with an unctuous hand towards the prisoner. "Lord Cassian of the Barren Peaks, if such indeed be your name, step forward!" he boomed, the words echoing with an unnatural resonance. Lord Cassian, with a grace born of long journeys over treacherous terrain, rather than any acquired courtly bearing, moved to the gilded cage before them, and fixed his grey eyes upon his accusers with a look half weary, half quietly amused. The proceedings began, as they often did in this singular realm, with an outburst from the Master of Revels, who, leaning forward from his perch atop a stack of cushions, let loose a peal of laughter so sharp and unexpected it might have been mistaken for the shriek of a desert harpy, right in Cassian's astonished face. "My little jester," said Lord Cassian, regarding him with a perfectly level gaze, "I often wonder if your merriment will not, one fine day, prove your undoing; for a man who laughs so heartily at the precipice of his own folly often finds himself tumbling headlong into its depths." "No levity, cartographer!" interposed the Grand Vizier, his face purpling with indignation; "remember, you are addressing His Most Unpredictable Excellency, the Master of Revels, First Entertainer to Her Divine Radiance, Empress Selene!" "Indeed!" replied Cassian, a faint, almost imperceptible smile playing about his lips; "Then all I have to say, is, that Her Divine Radiance has a curious preference for amusement, unless, perhaps, her intention was to surround herself with the most unsettling eccentricities in all the known world, as she herself is the most sublime embodiment of order and tranquility!" The Empress took not the slightest notice of this audacious compliment, not so much as a flicker of her obsidian eyelashes betrayed that she even heard it, but the Master of Revels shrieked with renewed glee until he was quite out of breath. "Silence!" shouted the Grand Vizier, shocked and indignant at this blatant impertinence, "and answer truthfully the questions put to you. Your name, you say, is Lord Cassian?" "Yes. Does your Excellency object to its resonance?" His Excellency waved down the interruption with a ponderous sweep of his bejeweled hand, and went on with severe, if theatrical, judicial solemnity. "You are the same who, but two cycles past, attempted to chart the Shifting Sands of the Eastern Wastes, a feat declared, by Imperial Decree, to be quite impossible?" "I had the distinct honour of sketching its ever-changing contours, and my only regret is, I did not complete the same good office for its companion, the Whispering Mountains, before I was so rudely apprehended." A ripple of nervous coughs ran round the room, and the Grand Vizier's cheeks acquired a shade closer to indigo. "These remarks are not only impertinent, but entirely beside the point. You are a cartographic heretic, let that suffice. Probably you were on your way to map the very stars themselves when you committed this transgression?" "He was," said the Master of Revels, wiping a tear of mirth from his eye, "I heard him muttering about stellar coordinates in the kitchens, only last night." "Very well, that is another point settled, and either of them is quite sufficient to warrant the revocation of your very existence. You came here as a spy, to pry into the unrevealed, and to document the undocumented--probably you were sent by the Duke of Shadowfell?" "Probably--just think as you please about it!" said Lord Cassian, who knew his case was as lost as a compass in a blizzard, and was quite reckless what he answered. "You admit that you are a spy, then?" "No such thing. I have confessed nothing of the sort. As I told you before, you are welcome to put what interpretation you please on my observations." "Lord Cassian, this is merely semantic evasion! You admit you came to observe and record?" "Well!" "Well, observing and recording constitute prying, do they not? Therefore, you are a spy." "I confess it sounds rather like it. What follows?" "Need you ask? What is the destiny of all who seek to map the unmappable?" "No matter what it is in other realms, I am quite certain what it is here!" "And that is?" "To be erased from all charts, to become a nameless drift, a blank space on every parchment--the fate of the Cartographer of the Lost Isles, in a word!" "You have pronounced it! Have you any reason why such a sentence should not be passed upon you?" "None; pronounce it as swiftly as you desire." "With the greatest satisfaction!" said the Grand Vizier, who had been vigorously scribbling on a scroll of luminous parchment, and now passed it with a flourish to the Master of Revels. "I have rarely known a judgment that brought me more profound gratification to record. Will His Unpredictable Excellency present that to Her Divine Radiance for her ceremonial seal, and then declare his sentence." His Unpredictable Excellency, with a grin of most exquisite, unsettling delight, did as instructed; and Lord Cassian looked steadfastly at the Empress as she received it. One of the gossamer-clad attendants presented it to her, kneeling, and she took it with a look half bored, half distantly amused, and lightly touched her signet ring to the luminous surface. Her obsidian eyelashes did not lift; no change passed over the calm, cold face, as serenely impassive as a glacier in a moonless night—evidently the charting or oblivion of the cartographer was less than a dust mote to her. To him she, too, was as nothing, or almost so; but yet there was a sharp, almost painful shiver through his spirit, as he saw that delicate hand, whose beauty was famed across ten kingdoms, so coolly sanction his erasure. But there was little time left for such introspection; for, as she pushed the parchment impatiently aside, and relapsed into her former haughty stillness, the Master of Revels leapt up with one of his most manic, ghoulish cackles, and began: "Lord Cassian of the Barren Peaks, you have been tried and convicted as a cartographic spy, and the impudent chronicler of the uncharted and unchartable; and the sentence of this court, over which I have the honour to preside, is, that you be taken hence immediately to the Labyrinth of Unmaking, and there have your name, your likeness, and all your works erased from the annals of all creation!" "And a mighty small loss it will be to the Emperor's libraries!" remarked the Grand Vizier to himself, in a sort of self-satisfied murmur, as the Master of Revels concluded his rather disquieting pronouncement by thrusting himself forward across the table, after his customarily erratic fashion, and breaking out into another of his shrill, unnerving peals of laughter. The Empress, who had been sitting as still as carved quartz, and looking as if she were in spirit a thousand light-years away, now started up with sharp, sudden grace, and favoured His Unpredictable Excellency with one of her most penetrating, jewel-like glances. "Will Your Unpredictable Excellency just permit somebody else to have a voice in that matter? How many more cases of 'unauthorized documentation' are to come on tonight?" "Only one," replied the Grand Vizier, glancing over a miniature scroll which he held; "Mistress Lyra's, for attempting to compose a symphony of the celestial spheres." "And what is Mistress Lyra's fate to be?" "The same as our friend's here, in all probability," nodding easily, not to say playfully, at Lord Cassian. "And how long will her trial last?" "Half an hour, or thereabouts. There are some harmonies in the matter that have to be investigated, and which will require some subtle adjudication." "Then let all the trials be over first, and all the erasures take place together. We don't choose to take the trouble of traveling to the Labyrinth of Unmaking just to see his legacy undone, and then have the same journey to undergo half an hour after, for a similar purpose. Call Mistress Lyra, and let this prisoner be taken to one of the oblivion cells, and there remain until the time for final erasure. Guards, do you hear? Take him away!" The Master of Revels' face grew an astonishing shade of bruised plum, and he jumped to his feet and confronted the Empress with a look so intensely ugly that no other creature of this realm could have assumed it. But that lady merely met it with one of cold disdain and utter detachment, and, keeping her dark, bright eyes fixed chillingly upon him, waved her slender hand, in her imperious way, to the guards. Those heavily armored gentlemen knew better than to disobey Her Divine Radiance when she happened to be, like a roused celestial dragon, on the "rampage," which, if her glittering eye and a certain unyielding set about her beautiful mouth spoke the truth, must have been twenty hours out of the twenty-four. A low, strangled sound, like the gnawing of rats in a forgotten cellar, escaped the Master of Revels' throat, and he raised a claw-like hand, as if to protest, to demand, to utterly forbid this capricious postponement, but no articulate sound followed, only a series of choked gasps that distorted his already hideous features into a mask of pure, impotent rage. He resembled, at that moment, some ancient, forgotten gargoyle, recently dislodged from its perch and still sputtering stone-dust from its ill-used maw, quite beside himself with the sudden deprivation of his anticipated sport.

The Empress, however, remained serenely undisturbed by this volcanic display. She had resumed her former posture of indolent majesty, her long, dark lashes once more veiling the enigmatic depths of her eyes, her head resting lightly against the carved back of her throne, a study in exquisite indifference. It was as though the very air of the chamber, thick with the lingering stench of fear and the acrid tang of injustice, held no sway over her serene, almost ethereal, presence. One might have fancied her a statue of some forgotten deity, carved from the purest, coldest marble, yet imbued with a faint, inner light that hinted at depths unfathomable and a will unbending. Her delicate fingers, adorned with rings that gleamed with the captured fire of a thousand stars, toyed idly with a silken tassel hanging from the arm of her regal chair, a small, almost imperceptible movement that spoke volumes of her detachment from the sordid proceedings unfolding before her. The Duke, recovering his composure with a visible effort, cleared his throat, a sound remarkably thin and unconvincing in the vastness of the hall. He glanced nervously at the Empress, then, with a forced air of authority, addressed the assembled company, whose murmuring had begun to rise, a low tide of whispered speculation and suppressed anticipation, like the restless lapping of waves against a rocky shore, waiting for the full force of the tide.

"Silence!" he commanded, his voice cracking slightly on the final syllable, which did little to quell the rising tide of hushed conversations, but rather, made it seem to ebb and flow with a renewed, albeit subdued, vigour. The Master of Revels, meanwhile, had sunk back into his seat, though with a distinct lack of grace, his movements still jerky and agitated, like a marionette whose strings have become hopelessly tangled, yet he dared not utter another sound, for the Empress's gaze, though veiled, possessed a chilling, almost palpable force that seemed to press down upon him, a silent, invisible weight of royal displeasure. He merely grumbled to himself, a low, guttural murmur that was lost amidst the general stir, and smoothed down the ruffles of his silken tunic with hands that trembled ever so slightly, a testament to the raw, unbridled power wielded by his sovereign lady.

"We shall proceed now," the Duke announced, drawing a long, shuddering breath, as if to fortify himself against the lingering awkwardness of the moment, and the palpable tension that still hummed in the air like an overstrung lute. He adjusted the spectacles perched precariously upon the bridge of his aristocratic nose, and consulted the roll of vellum once more, his brow furrowed in a manner that suggested intense concentration, though one might reasonably suspect it was more an effort to avoid eye contact with either the fuming dwarf or the unreadable Empress. "Let us then, without further ado, call upon the next accused. Guards, bring forth Mistress Lyra, formerly known as Lady Castlemaine."

A ripple, almost a shiver, ran through the assembled courtiers, a collective intake of breath that was both startled and intrigued. Her crime, the alleged poisoning of the Duchess of Sutherland, had been the subject of countless whispered tales and speculative glances for weeks, a dark rumour that had clung to the gilded walls of the palace like an unwelcome shadow. The fact that she, a woman of such renown and, let it be said, of such formidable connections, was now to face this mockery of justice, sent a frisson of genuine apprehension through even the most jaded of spectators. No one, it seemed, was truly safe from the Empress's whims, or the Master of Revels' insatiable appetite for vengeance, even if it was to be temporarily forestalled.

She was, indeed, a vision to behold, a creature of breathtaking beauty, even in the somber confines of a midnight court. Her gown, of a deep emerald velvet, was perhaps a little too opulent for a prisoner, but it clung to her figure with an elegance that defied the circumstances, revealing the exquisite lines of her form without being overtly immodest. Her hair, the colour of spun moonlight, was piled high in a cascade of intricate braids and curls, adorned with a single, trembling diamond that caught the flickering light of the torches and sent a thousand tiny rainbows dancing across the vast chamber. Her eyes, the colour of a summer sky at dusk, held a challenge, a spark of untamed spirit that refused to be extinguished by the grim realities of her situation. She was, in short, a queenly presence, even in chains, though there were no chains upon her, only the invisible bonds of accusation and impending doom. She made her way to the stand with a composure that bordered on the audacious, her chin held high, her gaze sweeping across the faces of her accusers and her judges with an expression that was part disdain, part weary resignation, and perhaps, a fleeting, almost imperceptible hint of amusement. The Master of Revels, despite his recent humiliation, could not help but glower at her with an intensity that seemed to drain the very colour from his already mottled face, for he, like all men, was not immune to the power of such beauty, even if he found it utterly exasperating in a female, especially one who dared to defy the established order of things.

The Empress, for the first time since the proceedings had begun, allowed her long lashes to lift, just a fraction, revealing the merest sliver of her dark, luminous eyes. Her gaze, cool and appraising, rested upon Mistress Lyra for a moment, a moment that stretched into an eternity for those who dared to watch, and then, with an almost audible click of her hidden will, her lashes dropped once more, returning her face to its accustomed mask of impassive beauty. No flicker of emotion, no hint of recognition, no shadow of judgment, crossed that exquisite countenance. It was as if she regarded the beautiful prisoner not as a person, but as a particularly intricate piece of tapestry, or a rare and curious jewel, to be observed and then dismissed. The court, however, held its collective breath, for that brief, almost imperceptible glance had been enough to confirm that the Empress, despite her outward indifference, was indeed paying attention, and that the fate of Mistress Lyra, no matter how dire, was ultimately hers to decide.

The Duke, clearing his throat with renewed vigour, attempted to reclaim the fragmented authority of his position. "Mistress Lyra," he began, his voice surprisingly firm, though it still lacked the resonance of true power, "you stand accused of a most heinous crime, that of poisoning Her Grace, the Duchess of Sutherland. Do you admit to this grave transgression?"

Mistress Lyra, who had now taken her stand before the green table, surveyed the assembled dignitaries with an almost insolent calm. A faint, knowing smile played upon her lips, a smile that hinted at secrets, at unspoken truths, at a profound understanding of the perverse game in which she was now entangled. And if the truth be told, my knowledge of poisons is no greater than my knowledge of celestial navigation, which is to say, none at all. I am, alas, a woman of simple tastes, and simpler accomplishments."
